utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Nice to be back after such a long spell out. So, we are happy also to hear Dr. Gow is fit now. We will come to him, so can we start now? Appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Dixon, Mr. Turone and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Edina Residovic appearing together with the Professor Eugene O'Sullivan on behalf of Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, my name is Zejnil Olujic, attorney from Croatia, appearing on behalf of Mr. Zdravko Mucic, together with my learned colleague, Mr. Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom. Before my next colleague introduces himself, we have an am application to make, your Honours, namely Dr. Zdravko Mucic would request this court to give him leave, after 12 o'clock, to be absent from the courtroom for the following reasons; namely in the detention centre premises a Catholic mass will be held. A priest is coming, and, since Mr. Mucic was unable to attend church services regularly in the past period, he would kindly request this honourable court to allow him leave not to be present to the testimony of Mr. Gow today, and he would authorise me to represent him fully in his absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of Mr. Hazim Delic, together with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Huston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning your Honours, my name is John Ackerman I appear here with Ms. Cynthia McMurrey on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we will grant the application of Mr. Mucic for his wishes to be absent, since he knows that it does not prejudice the defence. So the application is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Gow, might he be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you kindly swear the witness, please? Kindly swear him in. DR. GOW, (Sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Be at ease. You sit down. Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. Is it working?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is working. How are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We all heard about your accident and we were all very concerned, and I hope you have recovered and everything is okay. Good. Thank you. Where I want to begin this morning, Dr. Gow, is to discuss with you some resolutions of the United Nations Security Council and I want to pass some copies to the Registrar and to the court, and if someone can assist me with regard to that, I would be grateful. (Handed)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I hope you are ready now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am getting there your Honour. I need the Registrar to give me exhibit numbers for each of these documents, 1, 2, 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D30/4, number 1. Document number 2, D31/4, document number 3, D32/4, and document number 4, D33/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Dr. Gow, you now have before you four documents and up in the upper left-hand corner they are numbered 1, 2, 3 and 4, and that is the order in which we will talk about them. First I would like you to look at number 1. It is Resolution number 777 of 19th September 1992, and I am interested in having you focus on the second paragraph of that Resolution beginning with the word, "Considering ..." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In that paragraph it reads: "Considering that the state formerly known as the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has ceased to exist..." That is the language; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if another witness has testified to this Trial Chamber that because of that language of the Security Council, that it is clear that it was 19th September 1992 when the SFRY ceased to exist, you would not agree with that statement, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that the -- what the document in front of me does is recognise that the state formerly known as the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has ceased to exist. I do not think the document is saying that as of this moment it ceases to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the document addresses the question of continuing succession questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. It would be sort of a profound misinterpretation of this document to say that that is the date that we can fix as the end of SFRY, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be a misinterpretation to say that there were no continuing questions regarding the dissolution of the SFRY, but I think it would not necessarily be appropriate to argue that that was the date for the ending of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, if you were to take this as an argument then, because it refers to the continuing succession issues, then you would say that the SFRY continues to exist now as well because the succession talks continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would you look at document number 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On page 2 of that document which is D31/4, you will see a paragraph starting with, "Decides ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I just raise a matter? We do not have the numbers, 1, 2, 3 and 4. I do have copies of the Resolution, so if Mr. Ackerman would just tell us the Resolution's number, I can follow, but I do not have the numbers on the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This would be Resolution 760 of 18th June 1992, and the paragraph on the second page of that document starting with the word, "Decides..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is operative paragraph 6 in Resolution 761?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. Resolution 760, and in the upper left-hand corner you will see a paragraph starting with, "Decides ...", of the second page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, fine. This is the end of Resolution 760. I am with you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That paragraph refers, does it not, to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So on 18th June 1992 the UN Security Council is recognising at least the de facto existence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that being Serbia and Montenegro. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a political -- on a political level it recognises that there is something calling itself the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The reference to Serbia and Montenegro, I think, is a suggestion that the Security Council in this case as in many others before and after, did not want to prejudice a set of other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look now at document 3, that I have put before you, that is exhibit D32/4 and it is Security Council Resolution 757 of 30th May 1992. In that document I would like to refer you to the first full paragraph beginning with the word, "Noting ..." Do you see that? What the Security Council says there contained within that is language which says: "The former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia..." Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would be recognition on May 30th 1992 that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was no longer in existence, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it would be recognition that the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was in a process of dissolution and that by this stage, de facto, there was acknowledgement that that process was coming to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, when you refer to John Major as, "the former Prime Minister of Britain", you are not saying that he is in the process of relinquishing his Prime Ministership; he is just not it any more, is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that case, that would be so, although I would not necessarily be referring to him in the course of this evidence. What I would draw your attention to is opinions of the Badinter Advisory Commission to the International Conference which indicated that -- in an opinion in November 1991 indicated that the SFRY was in a process of dissolution, i.e. the events of the summer of 1991 had begun that process at which point in 1991 in November it was not yet completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the process of dissolution deals with issues surrounding matters that need to be dealt with when a state ceases to exist. It is not a process by which a state slowly ceases to exist and would you agree with me that the normal and common understanding of the phrase "Former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia" means that it is not in existence any more. And all we are dealing with are the issues surrounding that fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you were to ask me as an individual, then I would say my opinion at the time was that the SFRY had ceased to exist. If you ask me as an expert to assist in this matter I would say that others were of the view that there was a continuing process.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your view is that it had ceased to exist. Let me ask you to look at the fourth document now, which is D33/4. I am referring now to Security Council Resolution 752 of 15th May 1992. The second paragraph beginning with the words, "Deeply concerned ...", contains that same language, does it not: "The former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Your Honours, I would offer in evidence exhibits D30/4, D31/4, D32/4 and D33/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I would now like to talk with you a few minutes about the JNA, the Yugoslav National Army. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. During the period of time while the JNA were still the legitimate armed force of SFRY, would you agree with me that it had basically two missions; one was to protect Yugoslavia from external aggression, and second, to protect the state of Yugoslavia from internal insurrection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree with you entirely on the first point. I would amend your phrasing of the second, to say that -- and also you said, "Yugoslav National Army". In fact it should be the "Yugoslav People's Army". The "people's" has a specifically communist character --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- linked to the nature of the system. The same word, "nalodnja", can mean "people's" or "national", and I think in this context the people's element is significant, because the mission it was charged with in terms of internal -- of the integrity of the system was upholding the socialist order in the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And also preserving the territorial integrity of SFRY.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Preserving the socialist order of the SFRY as well as the territorial integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that would have been part of its legitimate job during the time that it was in existence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a role that it was charged with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And any fighting that might have gone on within SFRY while it was in existence would have gone on simply because JNA was carrying out that mission of preserving the territorial integrity of SFRY.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly would not say, "simply", that would be the case. It would have been a possible interpretation of some actions, for example, the JNA operations in Slovenia in June 1991 could possibly be given that interpretation. Some of the JNA commanders give the same interpretation to their operations in Croatia but I think, quite clearly and I think I have given in evidence in this Trial Chamber before, if not this one, then in others, there was a decision while the SFRY formally continued to exist in this period of process, where the JNA commanders decided not to seek to preserve the SFRY any more but to create the borders of a new set of territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We are going to go into that. You already cited the example that I was going to bring to your attention and that was the Slovenia example. You have talked, I think in your prior testimony in the Tadic case and in many of your writings about the compositional change that the JNA went through during 1991 and early 1992, and there was a significant change in composition during that period of time, was there not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, by the end of May of 1991 I think you have said that less than 3 per cent of the JNA at that stage was classified as something other than Serb and Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you may have made a mistake in saying 1991 when you meant 1992. As I recall the evidence went -- was with reference to March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You are absolutely correct. That is a typo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: March 1992 not May 1991, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think what you said in Tadic, in fact, was that the share of Serbs within the army by March 1992 had become 90 per cent, and non-Serbs had fallen to 10 per cent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you figured at that point that about 5 per cent would have been Montenegrin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this Serb component of the JNA at that stage contained a very high proportion of Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In March 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And some estimates have put that proportion of Bosnian Serbs as high as 80 per cent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible that some have put it that high. Certainly the figure would have been somewhere in the region of 50-80,000, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me quote for you something you wrote in Jane's in August of 1992, and ask if you agree: "Some estimates put the proportion of Bosnian Serbs in the YPA ..." That is the same thing as the JNA. "... as high as 80 per cent." I mean, those are your words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree that I wrote that and I think that is consistent with the answer I just gave. Some estimates would put that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in the same paragraph you said: "Certainly around 80 per cent of the YA in Bosnia remained there when the new Yugoslav state ordered its citizens in the army to return from Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are referring to the decision in May 1992 to divide the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. There certainly did come a time, did there not, when the JNA itself ceased to exist as a legitimate armed force of SFRY.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, I will avoid the word, "legitimate", for the sake of simplicity and brevity in this case, and say, yes, the JNA formally ceased to exist in May 1992, although of course, its ghost went on through the course of the Bosnian war and today the fact that the links are still essentially those of the JNA continue to be impediments in the Dayton process, as Ambassador Tardieu the American special representative pointed out a few months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You would agree with me, would you not, that generally speaking, an army can only be a legitimate army if it is serving a legitimate state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is a very complex question. It would depend on whether you mean, "legitimate", in the sense of legal or in the terms of a socio-political phenomenon and one which, unless you really press me on it, I would not wish to begin a seminar on which could last all day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your book, "Legitimacy", your first book, you talk about that issue to some extent, and you talk about an army cannot be a legitimate army if it is not serving a state that is in existence, unless it is in a belligerent status or something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that an army, all armies need states, and that the position of an army such as the JNA within a federal system and multi-ethnic country such as the SFRY was, needs to have a degree of social, political consent or alignment in order properly to be able to do the job which, as an army, it is primarily intended to be. It is a comment which I think essentially, General Kadijevic makes in his memoirs: no army in the world can exist without a state and explains that as one of their reasons for the change from protecting the SFRY to the new approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, so once SFRY ceased to exist, from a legitimacy standpoint the JNA necessarily must have ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure what you mean by, "a legitimacy standpoint". The JNA went through a process of disintegration as did the SFRY and both at a point ceased formally to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think as we go forward with the next series of questions, I might be able to clarify for you what it is I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There came a time when officers and soldiers who were members of the JNA, found themselves as serving different interests. For instance, there were former members of the JNA that became part of the Croatian army. There were former members of the JNA that became part of the Bosnian Serb Army. There were former members of the JNA that became part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army. There were former members of the JNA that became part of the FRY army, so that in a sense, you could speak of those who were fighting for each of those four armies, or part of each of those four armies -- in a sense, you could refer to them as, "former JNA".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question is, could you refer to people who had been in the JNA as former JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so, if someone refers in talking about the events that were going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina as -- refers in that context to a former JNA component, they might be talking about the Croatian army, they might be talking about the Bosnia-Herzegovinan Army, they might be talking about the Bosnian Serb Army because all of those had components of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that would be a misleading interpretation, to say they had individuals might be to say they had components, but I think normally the use of components would imply that they had the organisation and structural features of the JNA which would be a different question, in which case you could say that the VRS in Bosnia-Herzegovina inherited components of the JNA, in fact, retained many of the structures, whereas what you are talking about on the part of either the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the Croatian Army, or Slovenian Territorial Defence is a situation in which some people who had been members moved over, not to fight with the JNA or its direct successors, but with their opponents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at the Bosnian Serb rebels operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in many cases those units were pretty much intact with roughly the same officer component and enlisted component, and equipment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time of the formal division of the JNA, the units in Bosnia-Herzegovina simply were readopted as.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I think the position you took here today and it is consistent with the position you took in Tadic, was that the JNA ceased to exist in May of 1992. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was formally divided in May 1992. I think in this case and in Tadic and other cases, I have suggested that the division was, of course, not an entirely genuine division, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, in April of 1992 when the FRY was formed, that was in April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was proclaimed on 27th April 1992, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The 19th or the 27th. It is some time in April. In May of 1992 that was when the FRY announced this division that we have been talking about, in other words, the removal of all of the Serb Montenegrin component from Bosnia-Herzegovina, leaving in Bosnia-Herzegovina the Bosnian Serbs who were part of those former JNA units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you said, "April", but it was 4th May 1992, and Serb and Montenegrin personnel were generally formally withdrawn, although you will see sometimes in documents references to the continuing presence of those people, but essentially formally those personnel were withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was done by the FRY out of a sense that leaving Serbian and Montenegrin citizens in Bosnia-Herzegovina would lead to an adverse international assessment of the FRY; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this was based on a decision taken by the FRY Presidency on 4th May 1992 to evacuate those citizens of the FRY serving in the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this evacuation actually started and took place from 19th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding was that it was supposed to begin after 4th May, and to be completed with effect from 19th May 1992. It was not completed by that date, but that was the intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you consider what we have talked about so far this morning, and what we talked about the last time you were here, once the FRY had been declared as a combination of Serbia and Montenegro, then the authority of that government, and we talked about this last time you were here -- the authority of that government could not extend beyond the borders of Serbia and Montenegro. That was its territorial component. That is a poor choice of words, but that was the territory that the government sought to govern, Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have the advantage over me in remembering what we talked about in December. I think it is the case that Serbia and Montenegro formally declared the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with a view to the type of question we discussed, so as not to try to avoid being charged with the responsibility for the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina which -- it was playing a significant role in handling. Its proper legal and formal content was Serbia and Montenegro. I think if you talk about authority then it is clear that its authority also ran into the territories of the Republika Srpska Krajina and Croatia, and into the territories which were to become called Republika Srpska in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is one of the reasons why, throughout the international handling of the war people would go to Belgrade, much of the time in efforts to try to seek influence there. It connects with elements such as the -- when Belgrade formally recognised as the end of -- the SFRY is not going to be reconstituted, a certain -- continuing to assert, we have the SFRY's rights and responsibilities over the Serbs in Krajina, with the Republika Srpska constitution saying that it is part of this Federation and with the clause in the Declaration I think of the FRY constitution saying, "It is Serbia and Montenegro but others may join."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, from a purely legal standpoint, after -- I will agree with you on 27th April just for the purposes of discussion, after FRY was declared a state, consisting of Serbia and Montenegro, those citizens of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, were not any longer subjects of FRY, could not be subjects of FRY because they were subjects of other legitimate independent countries.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure if subjects -- I hesitate to talk about areas which are not really within my competence, but I am not certain that, "subjects", is the right term.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Subjects, citizens, whatever you want to call them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think the question really is that it became a matter of choice or the discretion of the authorities in the FRY as to whether or not it accepted those people as citizens. It continued to recognise and accept SFRY passports but not all of them. It was a process of selection on the basis of choice by the FRY for authorities as to whether or not they accepted people as being their subjects or citizens or whatever it is. As long as we are not going to be tied precisely to the term, we will agree, whatever we call it. I think the essential point is that it became a matter of their choice rather than choice of the individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you read the constitution of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You know how it defines who the citizens of FRY are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It defines them as the inhabitants of Serbia and Montenegro, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But that -- the inhabitants can be -- that is why I come back to the question of decision, the inhabitants of Serbia and Montenegro can be anybody that the FRY authorities decide to admit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, "inhabitants", in terms of the normal and customary usage of that word in the English language, are people who live there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, when did this constitution come into force, Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a copy of it and I would be happy to pass it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I just want the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It was April 1992. I do not have the exact date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 27th April 1992. I am sorry, may I finish the answer? I was in the middle of just saying...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a matter of choice, because there are many people who are FRY citizens who do not live in the FRY, just as many of the people in this room are not citizens of the Netherlands. It is a question for the decision of the state authorities. I know of people who originated in Serbia and Montenegro who the FRY authorities have denied citizenship and people who were not inhabitants of Serbia and Montenegro who have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. Serbia and Montenegro are well-defined geographical units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go now into a little more discussion about the May 1992 order where the Serbian Montenegrin citizens serving in the JNA were ordered back to Serbia, Montenegro. Are you familiar with a communication that the Federal Presidency of FRY issued on 21st May 1992 with regard to that issue? Let me pass you a copy of it just so that you will know what I am talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is there a copy for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it was given to you before his testimony last time. It is a document that up at the top has, "YU Society and the Law", check, and if you do not have it, Mr. Niemann, I can get you a copy immediately. It says, "Chronology of Events"...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There are several of those, your Honours, and the one I am referring to is the one that on the second page would contain the date 21 May. Can I get from the Registrar the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D34/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have that document before you now, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to refer you to that language on the second page of 21 May and contained within there you will find the phrase: "the Presidency of Yugoslavia has no longer any competence to decide on any military operation on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is an indication, is it not, at least from the Presidency of FRY that they have no control any longer over those citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina who are involved in the conflict there on behalf of the Bosnian Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, would you mind repeating?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is a statement by the Presidency of FRY that they have no competence to control and decide on the military operations being carried out in Bosnia-Herzegovina by members of the Bosnian Serb military.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a statement to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to show you now another document, and Mr. Niemann, this would be the one of 25 May, and this would be D35/4.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. What is different, your Honours, are the second pages. The first page on each of these is the same just to show the sources of the document, and then the second page is an extract from that source. Do you have that document before you now Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On 25th May, according to this document, the Presidency of Yugoslavia discussed the text of the UN Security Council Resolution of 15 May, and that was the Resolution where the Security Council ordered FRY to get the JNA out of Bosnia-Herzegovina, basically, as well as the Secretary General's report on Yugoslavia and a marsh of the Chairman of Security Council of 21 May: "The presidency notes that there are attempts without any justification to shift responsibility for ethnic war in Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It declares that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia will do its best to co-operate and participate in activities and decisions of the United Nations, that it is ready to engage in efforts of the UN and international humanitarian organisations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, appeals to all sides to allow de-blocking of the Sarajevo airport, openly calls all warring parties to immediately stop shelling Sarajevo, Mostar, and destroying other cities, distances itself from all unacceptable acts committed by certain military formations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the formations of Serbian people." That is what that text reads, is it not?.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a message on 1 June 1992 that Branko Kostic, the President of the Presidency of Yugoslavia sent to Boutros Boutros-Ghali, the Secretary-General of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at that moment, but if you have a copy...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe it will help in your recollection that that was a message to the Secretary-General saying that the 30 May Resolution of the United Nations was based on false accusations and false premises.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware that messages of that kind were sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, and in fact, on 1 June 1992, Kostic invited the UN Security Council to send UN observers to Yugoslavia to see what the true facts were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am prepared to take it from you that that is what he did. I recall that there was an invitation to send monitors to patrol the whole border at one stage, which was quite clearly made as being an unacceptable -- like an invitation which nobody was going to accept because it would have entailed so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me share with you another document, if I may. For your reference, Mr. Niemann, this is the 1 June document. Do you have this document before you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This is the date of 1 June 1992, and reads: "In his message to UN Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, Branko Kostic, President of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, stated that the UN Security Council had imposed severe sanctions against Yugoslavia, based on the false accusations that it had committed aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina. In order to get the real picture of the situation, Kostic proposed UN to send observers to Yugoslavia." That is the language of that document, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, and if you are interested in the language, I would just point out the discussion we had earlier, that the terminology, "President of the Presidency", is old SFRY terminology for a function which no longer actually existed after the declaration of the FRY. Sorry, that is a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Following the orders from FRY for FRY citizens to get out of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you know, do you not, that the last FRY citizens from the former JNA left the Marshal Tito barracks in Sarajevo on 5 June 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am prepared to accept that they left the Marshal Tito barracks on 5 June 1992. I do not recall the precise date for that event, but I am happy to accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to share with you now another document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But, sorry, can I just say, that they have left the Marshall Tito barracks but I would not say necessarily that they were the last FRY citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand. I have another document. I presume this would be D37/4.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann for your reference this is the report of the Secretary-General pursuant to paragraph 4 of Security Council Resolution 752. Do you have that now, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Secretary-General's report?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The second page of the document you have before you, which is page 517, at the bottom you will see in paragraph 6 a report on the Secretary-General detailing the -- basically the removal of Serb and Montenegrin citizens from Bosnia-Herzegovina. He says: "Most of these are believed to have withdrawn already into Serbia or Montenegro, some having been subjected to attack during their withdrawal. Others remain at various garrisons in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially in Serb-controlled areas, including two installations on the outskirts of Sarajevo, that there are personnel who have been blockaded in their barracks by the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or hostile irregular forces, mostly in the Sarajevo area." Then he goes on to talk about the 600 to 1,000 soldiers blocked in the Marshall Tito barracks at Sarajevo. He talks about, in subparagraph (b), several hundred JNA personnel in a logistic base at Sarajevo who were in the process of withdrawing during 27, 28 May and were attacked by Serb irregulars opposed to their withdrawal from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and several hundred JNA cadets blockaded in Pazaric, south of Sarajevo, who were finally evacuated on 29 May. In essence, what the Secretary-General is telling the Security Council at that point is that to his knowledge, based upon his sources, the Serb Montenegrin units remaining in Bosnia-Herzegovina or those who were anxious to but prohibited in one way or another from withdrawing, either by Serb forces or by Bosnia-Herzegovina having them blockaded in various locations. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the content of what you read.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that report, if you look at paragraph 17 on page 519, it is clear that that report was filed with the Security Council after the adoption of the Resolution of May 30th imposing sanctions on FRY for failure to withdraw Serb Montenegrin citizens from Bosnia-Herzegovina, because this Secretary-General refers to that decision in paragraph 17, does he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And it certainly can be read as saying to the Security Council pretty much what Branko Kostic said to the Security Council, "Your Resolution is based upon non-existent facts and therefore is improper", and the Secretary-General is basically saying to them the same thing, "Everybody who was allowed to leave from Serbia and Montenegro has left. The only ones there are being kept there against their will, and it is an interesting Resolution, Security Council. We hope that it has some effect on the international community's determination to end the fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and will make it easier to negotiate the necessary agreements." That would be a way to read paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose it could be a way. I do not think it is necessarily an accurate way to read it, to link it to what Kostic was saying. It simply says -- it reports in the earlier paragraph a number of things which have occurred primarily around Sarajevo. In the report, I think if you see paragraph 4: "Given the considerable restrictions on unperformed freedom in Sarajevo and elsewhere... it has not been to obtain completely authenticated information." So I think the Secretary-General in the report is to begin with recognising that the information about which he can provide concrete -- a concrete view, primarily about Sarajevo is there but that does not necessarily reflect the situation in the whole of the country, and there is a difference, I suspect, between the Secretary-General saying, "I have reported on a certain number of facts about which I know something, I do not know everything", and what Branko Kostic says which is quite clearly for the political purpose of trying to oppose the Security Council's actions which are because of the role that Belgrade is playing in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I would say -- you asked me before: did the documents say -- does it say Kostic says this; yes, it says Kostic said that. Is what Kostic said necessarily accurate is not what you asked me and I suspect maybe the answer to that would be, "not necessarily". So you have this question -- I mean, I do not know if you are going to produce the Secretary-General's report of 15 June but I think if you are then we will see when we get to that, there are continuing references to the presence of the JNA units, or rather of the elements of JNA from Serbia and Montenegro, still in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in spite of going beyond the 19 May deadline. So there is a kind of a series of elements in the situation which do not necessarily correspond with that kind of interpretation which links what the Secretary-General says here to what Kostic says, I would have thought. Also, behind all of this I think you should -- two things are always to be borne in mind. One is that Belgrade had consciously taken the decision for the purpose of disguise or deception of the intent, and so as to try to avoid being punished, formally to divide the army and leaving its wherewithal, as you described before yourself, the units, the components behind to prosecute this campaign essentially as proxies of Belgrade's campaign to create a set of new borders that we discussed with reference to Kadijevic, so in all of this I think you have to bear in mind the Security Council is firstly addressing that part of the question and Belgrade's responsibility for that situation, whereas in other cases, Slovenia, Croatia, the non-Serb parts of Bosnia and Macedonia it has actively withdrawn all equipment that it had, so it shall not fall into the hands of others and, where possible, destroyed anything that it could that was left behind, and add to that that I think the permanent mention of the Security Council probably have other resources for gathering information than those simply through their diplomatic and other channels of the report of the Secretary-General. I think all of that needs to be borne in mind. I am sorry, forgive me for...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, it is unlikely, is it not, that the Security Council would have known more about the situation going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina on May 30th than the Secretary-General would have known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, do you think we can stop here so that you can continue at 2.30 to allow Mucic to keep his religious appointment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me, right before we break so I do not forget to do it -- can I offer 34-4, 35-4, 36-4 and 37-4?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not understand what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am just offering as exhibits, four of these documents that I had not offered before, 34 35, 36, and 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I ask you, your Honours, for half an hour, because as far as I have understood, the security officers would keep our defendants throughout that time in the courtroom, so a half an hour break would give them the opportunity to go out as well. If the break is shorter than half an hour, then they do not have a chance to have a cigarette or something like that, so my request is, could we have a half an hour break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This break is more than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is until 2.30, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Oh! I am sorry, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will come back at 2.30. This will not take me long. (12.10 pm). (Luncheon adjournment) 19 20 21 22 23 24 25 (2.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Perhaps we can get your witness back to his stand. Just kindly remind him he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am so reminded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, it is all for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Dr. Gow, I have good news and bad news for you. The good news is that I have very few more questions I have to ask you and the bad news is that there are three lawyers coming behind me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have been waiting for that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With the help of the usher I have one more document I want to share with you. I have given you an extra copy for Mr. Niemann. Could I get the exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number, D38/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Dr. Gow, this exhibit is provided to you both in an English translation and in the original Serbo-Croatian which I think also shows an original signature. My question is, do you recognise this document? Is it a document that you have previously seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this stage, I would not commit one way or the other. I mean, it looks like documents that I have seen, but I cannot say -- I would not say without having something against which to check it that I had seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It purports to be, does it not, an order from the chief of the headquarters of the armed forces ordering the removing from Bosnia-Herzegovina of citizens of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and specifically listing the units that are to be moved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It appears to be something along those lines, although I take it from the translation that it is chief of the headquarters of the armed forces, that certainly the photocopy that I have here does not show that clearly on the original, but I am not... you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You do know that on or about 11th May 1992 there was such an order. We have discussed it earlier in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, there were orders concerning the redistribution of personnel and units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will offer exhibit number D38/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, that should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Dr. Gow, in June of 1993 you had an article published in Jane's and in the course of your writing in that article, it was clear to you that the army of the FRY was not at that time engaged in the fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not regard it as being a fair statement. I am not sure quite what you have that is written or how you are reading it, but I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before you go any further, then let me be fair and tell you exactly what you said, and if necessary, I can pull that article and you can confirm what I am saying and you tell me if that is necessary: "The declarations by Generals Stefanovic and Panic that the YA could enter the Bosnian or Croatian fray must be taken seriously. It may be that threats to use the YA in the case of any international intervention on the territory of the former Yugoslav state are rhetoric. However, with the Stefanovic approach clearly ascendant, there is every chance that the YA would undertake knowingly and reluctantly fruitless action against any potential intervention." I need to go on: "The YA's engagement in Bosnia is not inconceivable. At the same time, the Belgrade politico-military elite has been careful in testing the thresholds of international tolerance and probably would not go into action if it was thought there was a more prudent course." That is the quote.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that seems a very fair representation, and I think if you were to understand that and probably to have read it in context, there is a difference between the covert use of units of the VJ in addition to the elements of the old JNA left behind to operate as proxies, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the situation to which you are just referring, that is a situation in which there would be the possibility, under discussion from General Stefanovic of a formal and open commitment of the VJ, in this case written as the YA, the Yugoslav Army, to the fray. So, in addition to the use of those units left behind as the VRS, and the forces operating in support of those limited forces in a covert way, you would be changing the situation to one in which there would be open involvement in which the kinds of questions that we discuss from time to time in this Trial Chamber would not have arisen in the way that they do, and I think that the essence is to understand that in the context of that article, that is what is in question, the formal and open commitment of the VJ as a whole rather than any involvement in any presence. I think it is quite clear from the quote reference to testing thresholds, a key part of this whole strategy was to test thresholds, and part of the threshold was the idea that it was unacceptable, in the given circumstances, openly to commit forces and to admit that those forces had been committed, but it was conceivable that circumstances would arise where there would be no alternative but to do so in a larger way, and with an open commitment. If I may, I would also go -- I was not given a chance to answer the last question this morning which was about the Secretary-General's degree of knowledge vis-à-vis that of the representatives of the permanent members of the Security Council and whether or not I thought the permanent members would know more or less than the Secretary-General. I think it has to be said that with all due respect to what the Secretary-General can get to know through certain channels, it always has to be recognised that the permanent membership, in particular, of the Security Council is in a position through a variety of means, if it is government agencies, to establish what is going on and what a position is, and that kind of analysis is reflected inter alia in the memoirs of Warren Zimmerman who was US Ambassador to Belgrade at this stage, so I think to be clear about the understanding and where it comes from and what the Security Council members might or might not know. It is rather like the situation, vis-à-vis Iraq, that is going on around us as we speak. Many people might say, "Well, what do they know? What does the Secretary-General know?" I would take it as a very fair assumption that representatives of my own government and of your government know full well what is at stake and why the situation is the way that it is. Sorry, it is kind of -- the question was raised, forgive me for drawing you back to it at this stage, but it does seem -- it went unanswered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it is your position, then, that the members of the Security Council deliberately keep the Secretary-General in the dark about matters which they have instructed him to deal with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it would be a fair assumption that all governments do not share all things that they know with people at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your answer before your most recent explanation leads fairly naturally into the next question that I wanted to ask you, and that was this: it was to the advantage of the FRY, Serbia and Montenegro, to be seen as not involved in the war in Bosnia and to have it seen as a purely civil internal conflict, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was to the advantage of the FRY, if it could establish that that was the way in which events were seen. That goes to some of the documents you showed me this morning, the statements by Kostic and so forth taken from the Yugoslav official publication site, all of which were in the context of saying, "This is not our concern", because they did not want it to be seen to be their responsibility. The same with the decision referred to in May on which this document reflects. I would also just -- we went away from this quickly -- note that in the same document that there is reference in the second paragraph, on the second page, that if, for any reasons, the transfers detailed on the first page cannot be accomplished, then the Commander of the military district will decide what to do with them. I think if you had looked at a close record of what actually happened, a number of cases, the units concerned did not go to the destinations indicated here. It would be a matter for detailed examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to try something. The question that I asked you was: it was to the advantage of FRY, Serbia and Montenegro to be seen as not involved in the war in Bosnia, and to have it seen as a purely civil internal conflict. Is there any reason why you just cannot say, "yes"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did say yes, and expanded on the answer. I thought; forgive me if I did not, I thought that was the first part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it be possible if you agree with a question that I ask you, to just say, "yes", if it is a fair response?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, provided, your Honours, it is a fair response, because just saying, "yes", to a question such as, "Is it true that Belgrade had never had at any stage aspirations over Bosnia-Herzegovina?", in the context of some comment made by a politician could be, "Yes"; but an explanation is then called for as to why that would not be correct. So, I object to Dr. Gow being constrained to simply, "yes", "no", answers when it is clear and obvious that an explanation is called for as to why it may be a "yes", answer to the contents of some document or material, but that the reality of the situation is that it is not, "yes", at all, but some explanation is called for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when an explanation is called for, I have no objection, your Honour; I am just trying to move things along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not know why you should stretch this question too much. I think it is a matter of opinion, because he is not the pro tem government of Yugoslavia. Whatever he says is his opinion about it. He might say "yes" or "no".

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was also to the advantage, was it not, of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be seen as victims of international aggression because that government was trying to get international assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We discussed that in December, if you recall. That political situation with FRY and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina having an interest in matters being seen a certain way by outsiders makes it very difficult to give account to reports from either side about what was in fact going on on the ground, because you never know whether you are dealing with a political statement or a factual statement. Just as a general proposition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a general proposition, it could, but as a general proposition I think it would have to be treated with caution and it would really depend on the situation and what sources were available and the context and what might be said about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, for instance, you know that there are those who contend that Serb paramilitary groups were operating in Bosnia-Herzegovina under the direction and encouragement of the Belgrade government. You know that there are people who so contend, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do indeed. I would contend that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in the Tadic case when asked about that your answer was: "I have no specific knowledge of meetings between government officials and members of any paramilitary groups to establish strategy." Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your testimony in Tadic was this: "I have no specific knowledge of meetings between government officials and members of any paramilitary groups to establish strategy."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that is the record, then I am sure that it is an accurate transcription of the record. But if, "government officials", includes members of the JNA, for example General Stefanovic, then there were meetings, and also in the evidence presented, as far as I recall in the Tadic case, we used the personal evidence of Vojcem Seselj, one of the paramilitary leaders, about -- referring to his discussions with President Milosevic himself, so I am not sure. I mean, I think it is something which would have to be treated with care.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is totally fair and we are going to get into some more specific matters with regard to that. One of the problems that the international community in general had, and I am talking about during the Vance/Owen process, during the Lord Owen process and any efforts made by international organisations to try to deal with what was going on in Yugoslavia, was trying to figure out who was in control of what at various times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was a question of trying to sort out at some stages the degree of control that was going to be exercised. I think it was always clear that if Belgrade chose to exercise influence and control over those forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it could, which was demonstrated when finally the war came to an end, and on a number of occasions the head of the security service, Jovitze Stanovic was sent down to Bosnia and Belgrade's wishes came into effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me go back to a fairly early time, even before the fighting broke out in Slovenia. There was activity in Belgrade by the JNA in the formation of a new communist party; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the issuance of arrest warrants for the Croatian Defence Minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the deployment of tanks on the streets of Belgrade following speculation regarding the imposition of Marshall Law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Deployment of tanks on the streets of Belgrade following agreement of the Presidency, the State Council to do so, following a request from its Serb representative on behalf of the Serb authorities, in response to demonstrations on the streets of Belgrade on 9th March 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you said --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the question of the state of emergency came in the days after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you said about that, those three issues in the South Slav Journal was that: "Each of those demonstrates that the military action are governed by attachment to its Communist roots, and the absence of central authority in Yugoslavia." What I want to focus on is, "the absence of central authority in Yugoslavia"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it correct that that is what you want to focus on, or...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that these actions that we just talked about done by the JNA were done in the absence of authority. They did those things on their own.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not on their own. Because, for example, the deployment of troops on the streets of Belgrade was taken in conjunction with, as I said, on the authority of a decision of the Presidency which decision was arrived at through the request and the pressing of the Defence Secretary and the Serb representative, Borislav Jovic and equally that the moves towards a state of emergency afterwards were part of an arrangement made between Jovic and the Defence Secretary, Kadijevic, so to say, "on their own", would be wrong, and maybe if I were to rephrase what I wrote as the absence of central authority...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "Absence of central authority in Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would be maybe not the complete absence but the weakness of, and the fact that central authority was divided and at this stage you were in the run-up to the final break-up and the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So then what you said in the South Slav Journal was not wholly accurate. Is that what you are saying today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I say that it is a fair representation, but if you were to give it specific interpretation and context for something not to be written in the South Slav Journal, but for the purposes of the court which -- I think probably an element of fine-tuning would be required; then I would say "absence" would be the wrong word, yes, but it would not give you the wrong sense that central authority had broken down, was breaking down, and that there were certain events going on and the army was seeking to carry out the role you identified this morning in upholding the socialist order and finding ways to deal with elements within the system to try and address those problems of weakness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So, in all of your writings should we read them with a sense, in our minds, that you may have chosen the wrong word and not been as precise as you could have been with regard to your writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think you should do that at all. I am happy to say that in -- one of the things I recall from before Christmas is that you kept putting a lot of things to me and I was uncertain about them and then you rephrased them quoting from what I had written and I was far happier with what you quoted from that I had written than the way in which you had paraphrased things, and I think there is a degree of care in what I write, on the whole, and I cannot say that either what I say verbally or what I write -- I can never say that with retrospect I might not choose a different word here and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you are writing you certainly have an opportunity to review what you have written, maybe numerous times in the editing process, to try to make certain that you have chosen the right words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Often that is the case. It is not always the case, and sometimes maybe something written at one stage will look slightly different something like ten years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And by contrast --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But thankfully not too different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: By contrast, in testimony you give before the court you really do not have that opportunity to carefully review your words to make sure you are using precision. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have the same opportunity. As far as possible I take care in what I say and I try to make sure that what I say accurately represents what I would wish you to understand, and that the court -- if I am trying to assist the court I try to be as careful and accurate as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You certainly had control over the words that you chose in your writing in the South Slav Journal, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be perfectly honest I do not remember any more, but I certainly would have chosen a set of words in the first place. I feel -- I mean, forgive me but I fail to see quite what the relevance of all of this might be. Yes, I wrote something, I see nothing in essence with which I would disagree in that, but for the purposes of the accuracy of working in a court, I would say, "absence", was the wrong word, but if it would make everything easier I will go back and I will stick by "absence" and settle for qualifications within my own mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, just so that you will understand and I think I am quite certain you do, whether or not something is relevant is an issue for a judge to decide, not a witness; okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, but I think it is fair for me to understand what it is that I am being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me take you now to the fighting in Slovenia. You know what I am talking about when I talk about, "the fighting in Slovenia"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: During that short conflict there the JNA was acting largely on its own initiative with what it did there, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was acting largely on its own initiative, yes. It was deployed formally to give assistance to the Federal Police, but the action which it took was far beyond the authorisation, so I would say, yes, it was acting largely on its own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Your words again: "The YPA...[which is the JNA]... seemed to be acting largely on its own initiative in Slovenia." Do you want to change anything you wrote in, "Survival", in that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said, "no". Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. In that same article you said this: "After the EC mediators met in Belgrade on 29 June and presented their three-point cease-fire plan the Federal Army...[that being the JNA]... for its part acted without political authority and launched its heaviest assaults to date on Slovenia." You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree both that I wrote it and that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. There were even instances, were there not, that we can point to where the JNA itself had little control over what its own commanders were doing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true that there were instances in which JNA commanders appeared to be acting with a degree of local initiative and authority, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this was noticed and reported by EC monitors who were working in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was noted, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was admitted by the Deputy Defence Minister, Stane Brovet --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was admitted by Brovet. I would express by now a degree of caution to be sure how far, again in line with some of the other things, that was something said in the sense of they would not want to say the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Again, I think, the best way is for me to just tell you your own words. This is from a journal, RFE/RL which stands for something I have forgotten.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Radio for Europe/Radio Liberty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes: "In some instances the YPA...[which is the JNA]... had little control over its own local commanders as EC monitors reported and Deputy Defence Minister Admiral Stane Brovet conceded." Now, those are your words. Do you agree with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I agree that I wrote them and I agree, broadly, I agree with them. In retrospect I think I would interpret some of those things differently. That has to be seen as something written at a time, and I think, I would stress that most -- that as situations develop, not only I but other people begin to see pictures emerge which are not necessarily to be seen in a particular moment, and if you understand from the things we discussed before that part of the strategic approach involved the importance of disguising things which might actually be happening, and therefore attempts to give a sense of disorder and confusion, and it is conceivable that what might have been happening was not completely, as I wrote there and described, but as part of a pattern of known camouflage, if you like -- I cannot think of the right word for the moment to express it -- which is not to say that I think that that was always entirely the case. I think there was an element of confusion all round, that people were trying to work out at that stage what was happening, and as part of trying to work out what was happening, they drew conclusions which, in retrospect -- some of which might be true, some of which might be subject to re-evaluation which essentially is what I was saying in answer to the question before about the particular word I chose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that caveat that you just shared with us here in this courtroom was not one that you shared with your readers when you wrote that article for RFE/RL, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is true that I did not share it with them. I do not think it was something to be shared. It is not normal practice to share caveats of that kind. People write on the basis of the material available at the time. If material adds to understanding later, then it would not be wrong, first of all, to incorporate that additional material in understanding, and put it to use, and, secondly, as far as appropriate, to adjust the understanding. One of the things also, in fact, in that article to which you refer is the nature of the paramilitary groups and the way they were operating. I think it has become far more clear since then, the degree to which some groups which apparently were part of this chaotic environment, all ended up having connections to Belgrade official organs, which is evidence which emerged some time afterwards and which evidence has since been presented in course of testimony here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In October of 1991, the EC was trying to negotiate one of the many cease-fires that were negotiated in the Former Yugoslavia and came up in October with a plan that five of the six republican leaderships agreed to. Although? All Milosevic was being stubborn about it. And in discussing that in an article you wrote with a gentleman named Freedman, "Intervention Bands of Wickedness", you said: "In spite of whatever Kadijevic continued to say..." Well, I need to go back: "The existence of both Croatian and Serb extremist groups as well as a Federal Army whose operations in spite of whatever Kadijevic continued to say were beyond political authority, meant that a political agreement would probably not mean a prompt end to fighting." Those were your words in that article. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And to expand on that just a little bit, what you are saying is that, because the Federal Army and these extremist groups were operating beyond the political authority of Belgrade or other political authorities, any agreement entered into by the heads of the various republics may not mean much because they had no control over some of these organisations that were carrying on the battles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is -- from what I recall how you read it I think that is something which could be interpreted from it. That is something, again, which in the light of the subsequent publication of Kadijevic's memoirs to which I have made reference before, it becomes clear that the situation in that -- on that question was very different. The apparent lack of political authority was in fact part of a process, a two-fold process. One was a competition -- not a competition -- was part of the process by which the Serb leadership and the JNA's general alignment was being brought into one of common cause in the new project to create this set of borders we described, and the other is the degree to which it was always possible to try to make political agreements but with no intention of actually implementing those agreements because armed force would be used to prosecute a different cause on the ground. I think what we have to look at in this context is the idea that while political agreements were being sought and discussions on potential settlement were being conducted there was a conflict taking place on the ground, and that that conflict was -- the point of that conflict was to establish facts on the ground, which facts would then have to be dealt with as part of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you refer to Kadijevic's memoirs. Memoirs in the first instance tend to be self-serving, and so it is a bit dicey to rely on someone's memoirs to establish undeniable facts about what happened in a situation, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I would agree with the first part of the proposition that memoirs have to be -- well, always will have some element of being self-serving and in that context I would note that when Kadijevic's memoirs were published in Belgrade a number of those of a particularly Serb nationalist orientation who had previously criticised Kadijevic for being too Yugoslav put precisely that point, that the memoirs as appeared were self-serving, making it seem as though what he had been doing all along was the kind of thing that I guess they might have wanted, rather than what they thought he was doing at the time. I still -- and there are areas in which he expresses opinions about things -- I would presume were not ones that he actually knew about, but just it was his opinion. In those matters concerning military operations about which he did know something, I would expect that the material presented is reliable, and to that extent I would also say that material presented in other places, for example, the Jovic diaries to which I made reference, which may also in some lines have the same kind of self-serving purpose, still also contain the basic material which establishes what was happening from the people who were involved as the actors at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember an incident that happened in the time frame of October/November 1992 where Milan Panic who at that time was the Prime Minister of FRY, in an attempt to help ameliorate the situation going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina, agreed to allow the transfer of Bosnian Serb aircraft to Serbia for safekeeping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you remember that in negotiations with Lord Owen regarding the no-fly restriction and the almost certain efforts of the United States to enforce that, that Radovan Karadzic had agreed that the Bosnian Serb aircraft should be transferred to Serbia for safekeeping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, declarations or agreements of that kind were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, and you also know that the Commander of the Bosnian Serb Airforce, Major General Ninkovic, refused to transfer the aircraft because he said that could be a capitulation and not even Karadzic has the right to capitulate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You beat me to it. I was about to say that when you came in with a question. Yes. Although, again, I would point out that in all of these things it is possible to say one thing for political effect, but -- to have somebody else be seen not to be doing it, and either creating ambiguity or testing thresholds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is kind of the bottom line about all these things. It is trying to get hold of jello because you never know what is political and what is real. You have a difficult time distinguishing. That is a fair statement, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I do or that people generally might?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
