utterances.text: People generally do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People generally might, yes. I think that is fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I appreciate the time we have spent together and I have enjoyed it, and thank you, and I do not have anything more to ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Olujic, you are...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Dr. Gow. First of all, let me tell you, I hope that the length of the trials here at the Tribunal and in view of what you have been through -- we hear that you have been indisposed -- I hope that this will not disturb you. I will try to concentrate myself on what my colleague Mr. Ackerman has said, in order not to repeat things unnecessarily, and I think also in order to check certain things, check the authenticity of certain claims, because it has to be clear, Dr. Gow, that in the field of social sciences, unlike exact sciences, natural sciences, where everything can be verified, social science is always dependent on one's experience. It is empirical knowledge. Dr. Gow, during the chief examination in the Tadic case, among other things you claimed that there is a category of so-called, "Yugoslavs". Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made reference to statistical documents from the SFRY in which one of the ways in which people could categorise themselves was by the label, "Yugoslav".

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but Dr. Gow, the constitution from 1974 did not provide for them, but they also were undeclared at the census.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am getting drawn between the two versions. If I have understood correctly, all the peoples forming the States of the SFRY were regarded as Yugoslavs in the sense of being South Slavs, therefore that is why I think it would not be relevant to have them treated in the same way as state-forming peoples because they were all variants of being South Slavs. There was some part which I got lost between the end of your version and the translation and I wonder if you could just repeat the end of the question so I can be clear what the second part was, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Of course, doctor. The constitution of 1974, the last constitution in the Former Yugoslavia did not provide for the category of "Yugoslavs". However, during your chief examination in the Tadic case you said that there was a category of Yugoslavs as a nation. That is what is in the record. I therefore suppose that you are familiar with the contents of the constitution of the 1974 -- and I hope you would agree with me because this is not disputed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree with you on the question of the state-forming peoples for the SFRY because all of them from South Slavs, Yugoslavs. The question, as it appeared to come afterwards referred to there being no category for the Yugoslavs in the census where the information I produced was taken from SFRY statistics in which people in the census were given the opportunity to declare themselves as Yugoslavs and did so. Now, there is a difference between -- and you used the word, "nado", I think, to refer to Yugoslavs. The Yugoslavs in this case were not treated as one of the state-forming peoples but they were a category registered in the census so there is a distinction to be made between state-forming people in the constitution and the census, if I have understood what you have put to me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: That is precisely where the difference lies because after the census they were classified as, "undeclared". They did not declare themselves as Serbs, Croats, Slovenian, Macedonians or else they were simply put in the group of "undeclared citizens". Now, let us move further on. During the chief examination in this case, while you were examined by my learned colleague Mr. Niemann, on page 9247 you said that your work was focused on the Former Yugoslavia for the past several years. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it has been. Not exclusively, but it has been focused on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, could you be more specific and tell us since when have you been focused on that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From somewhere in the -- certainly from 1983 onwards, maybe from a little bit before, depending on -- these are difficult questions, I would not take as a starting point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: That means roughly about fifteen years.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and tell me the title of your doctoral thesis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid that I could not. I do not remember precisely, but it involved the words, "Legitimisation", and, "Yugoslav People's Army", and words of that kind. Some of that material went into the book "Legitimacy and the Military", to which Mr. Ackerman made reference earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You also said that you could read Croatian, or as you called it "the Croatian or Serb language". Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember what I called it, but I read in those languages, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Can you read Macedonian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I busk in Macedonian and other Slav languages from the base of it. I must say, I have read things in Macedonian, and I have drawn things from them, also in other Slav languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And how about Slovenian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same with Slovenian.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that we could also speak in one of the South Slav languages, that you would need the English language, or do you mean that you can only read these languages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it should be necessary, we could speak Serbo-Croatian, but I think it would be better for me to continue in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Dr. Gow, have you read the laws of the SFRY in one of the South Slav languages or in the English translations, when you studied the legislation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess, if you are making references to things like the constitution, in both, at different times, depending on what it was and when and what was available, but always taken when used -- taken if possible from the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Mr. Taylor who has written a lot about the Austro-Hungarian monarchy? The name of the author is, "Taylor".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which Taylor?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: A.G.P. Taylor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A.G.P. Taylor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, could you supply us with the list of publications that you have read in relation to the history of the Former Yugoslavia and its peoples? Would that be asking too much?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suspect that it would. I mean, I could try and find ways to provide a list, if you really wished, but I cannot imagine how I would manage to make... I certainly could not provide one just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Later. That is what I thought. Could you also provide us later of course, with a list of books and articles that you have written about Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure, but I believed that that had already been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That has already been provided for, your Honour, and I wish to address the court at some stage, if this request for everything he has read is pursued because we will be here for the next two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Please. Go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I thought I had finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: All he has read on a particular subject? How can you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No, no I thought...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you really need that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I meant the list about articles written about the Former Yugoslavia, but we have just heard that the witness could do that, so if necessary, I think -- and that is the reason why I ask him that -- I think it would be good if he could provide us with that. I did not mean right now, of course, but let us move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, but if I could just -- I think be clear, my answer was that, yes, and I was under the impression that that had already been done and I think Mr. Niemann confirmed that such a list had already been passed to the Defence, and I suspect that that was of assistance to Mr. Ackerman in preparing his cross-examination, but, I mean, if that is incorrect then I am sure it can be dealt with. (3.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the examination-in-chief and during the cross-examination by Mr. Ackerman you said, among other things, that the course of the crisis in the Former Yugoslavia brought about a collusion of the former JNA and the Serb cause. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct that I gave evidence to the effect that, as this process was taking place, there was collusion between the Serb leadership and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, my question was: could you be more specific in respect of time? When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was happening over a period of time. I would put the -- that is one of the most critical movements being in the early part of 1991. I know there are people who would say there was complete collusion from an earlier stage, and whilst I would not absolutely exclude the possibility, I think the evidence suggests that it was a process evolving, and I think, in answering Mr. Ackerman a little earlier, I spoke of the arrangements in March 1991, first of all by which the Serb leadership got armoured personnel carriers, which we referred to earlier as tanks, to be deployed on the streets of Belgrade. I think maybe there were some tanks as well, and following that circumstances in which the JNA, acting with the Serb political leadership, tried to get the State Council, the collective presidency of the SFRY, to declare a state of emergency, primarily to create a state of emergency in Croatia, but the question throughout the territories of the SFRY, and there was a meeting held, I think two meetings held, I think on 11th and 12th March 1991, at military headquarters in Belgrade, where General Kadijevic with the support of Borislav Jovic put these questions to the State Council. The State Council was divided, and did not agree to implement this state of emergency. This process of collusion, collaboration, whatever we might call it, then continued, with an arrangement between the Serb leadership and Kadijevic whereby Jovic would resign from the State Council. Jovic at that time was the Chairman of the State Council, creating a vacuum, something along the lines of the absence of central authority I was discussing with Mr. Ackerman earlier, which maybe was somewhere in between a complete vacuum, but certainly to create a situation in which that authority was not there, and this arrangement was then that Kadijevic would act with the army to declare a state of emergency. For reasons which I think we probably cannot be absolutely sure about, but I would suspect mainly go to Kadijevic's own lack of confidence or conscience in that situation, he did not go ahead with that intended action, and subsequently shortly afterwards Jovic took his place again in the State Council, in the Presidency. So I think that is one clear example of the point where this collusion is coming closely together.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Let us go back a little further, 1989. Because you have read a lot about the Former Yugoslavia, you know that there was a celebration of the 600th anniversary of the Kosovo battle in that year. So you are familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, do you know, to whom did the JNA generals report during that time, during the celebrations? Was that Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The JNA -- Kadijevic was a member of the Federal Executive Council, the government, and would report within the government, but primarily the authority over the JNA was by the State Council, the collective presidency. I think at that stage the Chairman of the Council was the Slovene Janes Stanovjic, if I recall correctly, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Stanovjic no, never. Maybe Danovzcek.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought it was Stanovjic but maybe it was Danovzcek. I thought Danovzcek came afterwards, but never mind, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So if we could agree on the fact that the JNA generals at that time reported to Milosevic in 1989, what would that mean, and what was Milosevic at that time in Yugoslavia? He was the President of the Serb Presidency, at that time; am I not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me be clear first of all that we are speaking hypothetically, that it is not a matter of fact that we agree that the JNA was reporting to Milosevic but we are speaking hypothetically that, had the JNA been reporting to Milosevic, then what would the situation have been?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I do not think you have understood me properly. The generals did report to Milosevic or saluted to Milosevic in 1989, but we will move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, are you meaning that at the celebration in Kosovo Polje they saluted? Fine. We can agree on that. I thought it was a question of authority and command and to whom they actually reported in a formal sense. Yes. But I do not think that should be taken too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, if a celebration that has an internal Serb character was put to the level of the state, and if the generals are saluting not the person who is leading Yugoslavia but the President of the Serb Presidency, then of course this means what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that it does because I am not sure what you take it to be that I just said, but I think, as I recall it, there was a particular question at the time about this, essentially, what could be regarded as Serb celebration --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Olujic, how is this all relevant for our purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is important for establishing the relevant facts, the decisive facts. We can see here that Dr. Gow, he has been presented here by the Prosecution, and he has been questioned about all kinds of things and we have to check them. We have to confirm all the facts that can be applied to our case, that can be relevant to our case, especially in relation to the structure of the state itself, and when the state actually ceased to exist. We have abandoned one commission on one side and then the actual beginning of the process on the other. Dr. Gow is a specialist in the area. He speaks South Slav languages and I would like him to answer to me, to tell me since when this process has been going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: ... but they must be saluting senior members of the Council of State so how does that really matter to whom they salute? They may be saluting a number of persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but at that time Milosevic did not represent the whole state. He represented one of the republics, namely the Republic of Serbia. Since Dr. Gow has assisted us in this matter as much as he was able to, I shall no longer dwell on this and I would like to move on, with your Honour's permission.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, I would be quite happy to move on as well, but I was about to finish a point in assistance which may help clarify exactly the point raised by the learned judge, that it was essentially a Serb celebration but one put into a federal context, and the point I was going to make precisely, and this is why I raised the name of Stanovjic before, was that there was a significant political discussion in Slovenia because of events in Kosovo as to whether or not Stanovjic should also be there as one of the representatives at this celebration, and also, I suspect, receiving salutes, but I think that may clarify what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, are you sure that the aim of the aggression in Bosnia-Herzegovina was simply to take some of its parts or was there something else in the background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not entirely sure what you mean by, "something else in the background". I mean I would be quite happy if you could give me a guide as to what you might mean beyond the first part of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, if one might speculate, he is trying to ask if you have other reasons, other than your first ones, why the aggression took place. Any other reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- what I think I have said -- I am not sure. I do not want to go in the wrong direction, but I think I have said many times that there was a campaign to create this set of territories, a new Yugoslavia, and that that would be a new Yugoslavia essentially built around the Serb people, for the Serbs, and as a consequence of that there came to be what is known as "the practice of ethnic cleansing".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, you said this morning that the JNA was involved in the process of refining the boundaries of the new Serb state. If I remember correctly this morning you said something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, I said something to that effect which was the project to create the new boundaries of what they would regard as a mini -- a new Yugoslavia. They would not call it a Serb state but it would be a set of federated territories involving Serbia, Montenegro, the lands in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia, and possibly at some stage it would have been thought also Macedonia, and that within that, in the lands in Croatia and Bosnia, there was clearly an effort to create those sets of territories in a way in which control could be exercised by the removal of people who might resist the new arrangement. I hope that is of assistance to your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, it depends on counsel, whether that satisfies your question. Are you still needing an improvement on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No. Thank you. As far as that is concerned. Do you know, Dr. Gow, that at that time certain official persons claimed that it was anti-constitutional and illegal for the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to demand independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that there were people who said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the point is that Republika Srpska was formed in support of Belgrade and as a form of threat? Would you agree that it was the first to start inflicting blows and to threaten with the destruction of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if it embarked upon the road of independence, so that Republika Srpska varied in its ambitions from the minimum to the maximum but it was always guided and instructed from Belgrade, and that this support was not limited to moral support alone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is rather a lot in there. Essentially, I would be in agreement that what came to be called the Republika Srpska was part of this project to create a new set of federated territories, of which Belgrade would be the capital, essentially for the Serbs, and that whilst I think there were periods for political purposes in 1993, 1994, possibly the Bosnian -- certain political leadership was given room to make decisions for itself, it was always in the broad context of this project that it was acting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is only part of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, there was a lot in it. I remembered as much of it as I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Counsel wanted to know whether they were not the first to inflict the blows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it would be fair to say that the onset of major armed hostilities on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina stemmed from this strategic approach which is to say that it would be a matter of very close investigation to establish exactly who fired which first shots where in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There are some claims that Croats fired the first shots in Herzegovina but without getting distracted by those elements I think the main thrust of the armed conflict was the use of armed force in pursuit of the project to which I just made reference: the creation of this new Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But you agree also that Republika Srpska was the first to threaten to destroy Bosnia-Herzegovina if it embarks upon its road, on a road of independence which would entail an entire organisational structure and everything else. Thank you. Do you agree that it was always guided and instructed from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I refer to my earlier answer which is that I think it was always part of a project which got essential guidance from Belgrade but there were times when I believe for political purposes the degree of control exercised was not as strong as it was at other times. So, in 1993, 1994, for political purposes, Belgrade gave scope for the Bosnian Serb as far as possible to appear to be acting independently and I suspect that in some cases they were, but whenever Belgrade wanted to it could and did take control. So ultimately, the project was always that conceived and implemented -- conceived and run from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I will come back to the second part of your question, but I am satisfied for the time being, and thank you. Shall we now move on to the question of Konjic which you referred to at length during the examination-in-chief and Mr. Ackerman's cross-examination. Could it be said and would you agree that the tempora criminis, there were many different formations in Konjic at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the period in 1992 to which we made reference, yes. There were different armed formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In the relevant period of time, that is from May, or maybe April, from April until October 1992. Would you agree also that those formations were not fully organised in the military sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I recall the evidence-in-chief that I gave so long ago now, I think I was making the point that there was a process of formation taking place for the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that elements of organisation were being developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that there was no joint command in that process of formation, that is the time we are talking about, not later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could, I would ask you to explain what you mean by, "joint command".

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What I mean is a chain of command, subordination, hierarchy, ranks, rules, uniforms, everything else that makes an army an army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I asked because there was a joint command formally created between the Croatian forces in the Konjic area and the territorial defence forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If you were talking about the overall command structure of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was evolving. It was based around some of the elements of the territorial defence structure. It was primarily being created around the framework of the Patriotic League which I made reference to in evidence-in-chief. There was some form of a chain of command, but I think it would become, as I think I said before -- it was something which was not in position in the way that you would expect in a regular armed force that was well-established. It was something which was developing, and which was only formally really achieved some time towards the end of the period you suggested, in November. But it was being achieved throughout the year and there were clearly elements of hierarchy and of command, although the use of ranks had not been formally adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So, we can agree that there were no prescribed uniforms, rules of combat did not exist, rules of duty, that there were no ranks, all the other things that if enumerated, so you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some of those things in some ways and some of them there were not. It was an evolving situation and as far as I understand it, most of those things were in the process of being developed, creating those structures of authority and hierarchy. In terms of the documentation on one of the questions we discussed in December, I believe, is the process by which in a situation of a number of armed forces, the role of co-ordinator came to be relevant and then after that the way in which tactical group formations had been adopted and used, response to the relative absence of an overall complete hierarchical normal command structure, the way that a tactical group commander had then been given responsibility and command authority for all units in a particular area of operation, unlike a conventional use of tactical group and then after that the way in which the tactical groups had given way to the formation of the core structure for the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so overall, you see this process of evolution and consolidations of command and control authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: That is why I am asking you this, because my next question actually relates to your answer. Could you tell us whether, in any army there exists this rank of co-ordinator, as a rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of the term, "co-ordinator" being used to denote a rank, it denotes a function, rather like Commander In Chief is not a rank within the armed forces but a function which is usually served by somebody of the most senior rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But the rank of co-ordinator does not exist. We can agree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, do you remember of any conflicts among the Muslims in that same period of time in the region of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall there being armed conflicts between Muslims in the area. There was clearly some kind of political conflict between -- when Mr. Dalic was co-ordinator. Again, this is not from expertise really in the area of Konjic it is just from some of the things that I have seen. I think I have said, I got the impression that there was an argument going on, at least, between Captain Ramic and Mr. Develic, so if by that you mean conflict between them, yes, if you mean armed conflict I am not aware of any armed conflict between Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me doctor, do you know anything about MUP having its own command which did not recognise others? Could we agree in that statement, that the MUP had its own command, but that this command, under no circumstances recognised other commands such as the command of the army, the territorial defence and the commands of other formations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I presume that again you are speaking in the same period.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Always, about that same period, yes. I am sorry if I did not make myself clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just want to be clear about answering. The interior ministry forces were one of the three elements which fed into the creation of the Bosnian army. It was a separate strand with its own separate lines of authority to begin with, but it was one of those elements as had been the case in Croatia which came to form the army, so I do not think I would agree that it never accepted authority or commands in other ways, but I would accept that to begin with it was a separate line of authority, a separate organisation and line of authority operating, but being brought into this overall framework that would become the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not the MUP in its entirety but those armed elements, relevant to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Certainly later on, but then at that time in addition to the territorial defence, the Ministry of the Interior forces and other formations that existed in the area at the time, I think that it can be ascertained that in that period of time MUP did have its command, of course, but this command was not incorporated, not co-ordinated with other commands, in other words they they were accountable to themselves. They did not recognise other commands because they were not operationally linked, in fact, with other commands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I understand it, that was the formal case, but also there were provisions being made in line with the old general people's defence doctrine which I guess to some extent was being used as a basis for MUP units to be assigned to, or to work with, to be co-ordinated with the territorial defence units. I think the key thing to stress is that there were separate elements, but all were being brought together into one formation, but it was a process.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And that is only your conclusion that you yourself are making. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I am not clear what you are asking me. Yes. It is the inference that I have drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Your Honours, with your leave, perhaps we should have a break now, or shall I continue with my cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, you may not. We will have a break and come back at 4.30. (4.00 pm) (Short break) (4.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have the witness? (Witness enters court) Continue, Mr. Olujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Dr. Gow, you are familiar with the international war law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am familiar with the existence of a body of international humanitarian law and laws of armed conflict. To say I am familiar with them, I do not know. I know something about the content, but I would not profess to be precisely expert in them or something of that kind, or to give comments. I mean, I am happy to discuss them as an individual who is aware of some things, but not in the sense that I would presume to pronounce.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But if I ask you some facts about the international war law, you would not mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome to ask me questions and as far as it is within my competence to answer them, I will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Gow, do you know anything about the sort of reflection of the international war law in the Former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that that is a question I am competent to answer, as far as I have understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Gow, you have had very successful co-operation with the ATP, am I not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have had co-operation with them. I am not sure -- it has largely been a good experience; whether it has been successful, I think, is for others to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I have read some of your previous testimonies, and I would like to ask you whether the ATP has been satisfied with your work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object!

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is for Mr. Niemann to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You would not have heard from him if he was not satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, your function here as an expert witness, is it not more, at least the way I understand it, to inform this honourable Tribunal about certain circumstances, including history, law and politics. Could we say that? In other words, Dr. Gow, let me illustrate my question. You are not a forensic witness; I mean, you do not have to establish certain facts and the scene of the crime and so on. You are here to instruct, describe certain situations in this particular case, in the territory of the Former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I understand my role, and I would assume that everybody else in this room understands what the role is far better than I actually do, it is to assist the Tribunal by providing material upon which to establish an understanding of the context in which alleged crimes were committed, and that that material may be relevant to whether or not the Statute, or some parts of the Statute can be applied. That is my understanding. I would not profess to say for sure that that is what the role is, if somebody told me it was otherwise. But, if I may, the point you made about forensic evidence, I mean, I understand I am here as an expert to assist the Tribunal rather than as a witness to events in Konjic in this case or as somebody who has specific knowledge of Konjic or as somebody who has made forensic examination of Konjic. I am somebody who has a broad understanding of the context and uses that broad understanding to provide points of contact with what I know about Konjic which is of course relatively limited and only on the basis of materials that I have looked at here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And of course we are treating you here as a scientist, so let me ask you, as a scientist, as a scientific argument, your claim during the examination-in-chief, the intention of the JNA to divide itself in officers of Serb origin and others, you said it was not merely your opinion. Does that mean that you actually base your opinions on the opinions of others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is true that at times I base my opinions on discussions with others. I think I made that clear a long time ago, but I think I made that clear at the beginning of the testimony, that I was giving along with material from other sources, documentary material, both things from published sources and elsewhere that I have gathered, documents that I have seen here in the Office of the Prosecutor; I base it on a whole range of sources of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And do you base your opinions on the positions of the Prosecution as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not, because I am not quite sure what the positions of the Prosecution are. I know that the Prosecution has a case to run, and that within that there might be requirements, but I base my opinions on an evaluation of the material that I see and my understanding of the situation and the events, but I understand that obviously the Prosecutor invites me to come to act as a witness, because that -- the nature of that evidence will be presumed to be of some benefit to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, Dr. Gow, you mentioned that it was very important what Mr. Jovic was saying. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is very important to take what Jovic says about decisions and events into account, because he was instrumental in that process taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that he had personal interest and that he played one of the key roles in those events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I would refer to my previous answer. I think I was saying that he was instrumental in what was taking place, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you not think that he should be afraid for punishment, of a punishment for his acts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a rather difficult philosophical question. Without knowing about the character of Jovic, I would not go too far in giving an answer to it. In a practical sense, then, I think it would be a decision for others to decide whether or not the content of what Jovic reveals would be cause for him to be fearful of the kind of actions you suggest, but I would have thought it indicates that, were appropriate circumstances to emerge, then this would be a factor which might lead to his being fearful, but that is a very difficult question to answer. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You have actually not answered it. You have not answered the question. So what is your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is very difficult and I thought I had done my best to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But it is an inappropriate question for him to have to deal with anyway, your Honour. It is not for him to be determining whether somebody should be fearful of prosecution or being guilty of something. I mean he is an expert witness here to comment on events, not to determine people's guilt or innocence. In my submission, your Honours, it is entirely an inappropriate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He does not know. Do you know whether he is fearful or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it is a factual question as to whether or not he is fearful, then I have no idea as to whether or not he is fearful, but I thought the question was one more of supposition than of fact, but if that is the case then I am quite happy to say, no, I have no idea if he is fearful.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What I am interested in, Dr. Gow, is the following: if your conclusions, conclusions that you drew from the diary of Mr. Jovic and you spoke about that during the chief examination and cross-examination -- if you have not used your conclusions in the Tadic case, why did you use them now, now that Moslems and a Croat are being tried?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the question that Muslims and a Croat are being tried has nothing of bearing on the use, and the use of the diary is to reinforce that which I said in evidence in the Tadic trial, at which point I made reference to the actual interview tape from, "The Death of Yugoslavia", materials in which Jovic gives himself in his own words -- says these things, but what was not there in the use of the tape or in my evidence at the time, was to fix the point in time as being 5th December 1991. We were just -- I was just saying it happened before and it was really to reinforce that point, and if you are asking me: would it have been better to have introduced the diary extract with the specific date at that time, then I would say, "Yes, I suspect it would have been", but... well, I did not choose to use it at that time because I had not -- I thought the material being presented would make the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I will be frank with you, Dr. Gow. I have not read that diary. I think it is completely irrelevant because I am familiar with the thinking and acting of Mr. Jovic, but I am sure he is trying to impress everybody about himself and accuse others and now I would like to know whether the fact that the use of his diary in this case, the case of Celebici, not in the case of Tadic -- has there not been a disruption of balance, because we have two approaches to something that should be identical in terms of scientific truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may say, I have a problem with your use of the term, "scientific truth", and then if I may just put that to one side, I can say that the only difference between the evidence presented is that the use of the diary specifically locates the date in a way which the interview tape does not, and in which the way I presented the use of the interview tape in the Tadic case did not. So I do not think it really creates any question of a difference of either two interpretations or a difference in balance. It simply locates a date and reinforces the point that was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief you spoke about the creation of Yugoslavia. Do you know who Vuk Stefanovic Karadzic was? Do you know what he said about Croats and their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps you would care to assist me by suggesting what you have in mind. I can think of some things but I would not...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: He said that all Croats were actually Serbs by ethnic background. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He regarded them as Serbs, as Serbs of a different religion who did not necessarily realise, I think -- that was the way he put it -- that they were Serbs. I think it was a general expression for most of the South Slavs. There was a perspective that all should be seen as the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that the celebration of his birth was one of the chief events while Milosevic was climbing to power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to say I had not registered it as one of the chief events in Milosevic's rise to power, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Dr. Gow, that in 1989 there was an attempt to transform on the 1st December, that is the date of the creation of the kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenians who did not recognise any single nation, that there was an attempt to create this, to turn this into a single national holiday, all-Yugoslav holiday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1989, did you say? I do not recall that being specifically in 1989. I know that there was discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Dr. Gow, that in the old Yugoslavia it was only allowed to carry Serb flags, a Serb banner as a church banner, but still it was the banner that was carried publicly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I am not clear what you mean by, "the Serb flag". Do you mean the flag of the Republic of Serbia or another flag?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No, I mean the Serb flag with their emblems. That was the only flag that could be openly carried out in the old Yugoslavia whereas other flags could not be displayed publicly for holidays and so on, but if you do not know, it is not really important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... to the use of those kinds of flag. I mean, the flags of the republics I have seen being carried, but if there is a specific type of flag, then it is not something which has fallen within that which I have looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, Dr. Gow, you testified that the Republika Srpska included in its constitution that it was part of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And did it, ever since the beginning, it threaten to secede from the BH, if the BH in turn secedes from Yugoslavia, not only to annex the parts in Yugoslavia but also to prevent the independence of the BH? Let me make myself more clear. It was the same as in the case of Republika Srpska Krajina in Croatia. Ever since the beginning it had only one objective, the preservation of the SFRY. Only here something different happened because of the events in the international community, Milosevic agreed to dissolve Republika Srpska Krajina, that is the one in Croatia, but not Republika Srpska. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, it is very difficult because you put rather a lot of information into the question. I have to recall it all and try to treat it. I would agree that -- with the proposition that the approach in the Republika Srpska Krajina and later with the formation of the Republika Srpska were broadly the same process, and part of the same approach. I would also agree that it is possible, that if it had been possible to hold together the SFRY, then there are those who were involved in pursuing that project who would have preferred to do so, and I think particularly that goes for senior figures in the JNA. I think it becomes a little bit redundant to discuss the ins and outs of those things too deeply when the fact is that events took a certain course and that once the dissolution of the SFRY was being acknowledged, in response to that the JNA acted in co-operation with Serb political leadership and security forces to put into operation this plan, and the plan which would take some of the territories from Croatia and from Bosnia and Herzegovina, but again within that, I think for the JNA generals, such as Kadijevic, if it had been possible to keep the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina and something more of what they regarded as Yugoslavia, then I would expect it to be likely that they would want to do that, but I cannot say for sure whether they did or not. I would say that it was just something so highly improbable in the given circumstances that further discussion of it is really rather immaterial, but if I am wrong I am happy to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell us, doctor, please, to follow up with what you just said, do you know what Milosevic said when international pressure eased in 1991, 1992 and how he justified his aggression against the Republic of Croatia? Do you know that he said that the whole world was aware of Nazis marching again and that the world would soon turn against them and destroy them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall being specifically aware of Milosevic as having said that. I do recall, for example, General Kadijevic giving expression to the idea that -- this idea of what he called, "the Fourth Reich", Nazis on the move again, and he was doing this even at the meeting at the military headquarters on March 11, 12, or thereabouts to which I made reference before the break. Again at that meeting, he spoke of the plan which is being unveiled and hatched from, yet again, for these powerful external forces seeking to break up Yugoslavia. I mean, yes, he said -- he was clearly somebody who voiced that kind of opinion. What I would say is that in January 1991, Milosevic at a lunch with the ambassadors of the European Union member states made it clear to them that if Yugoslavia was to break up, then this kind of action would take place, without, I suspect, going into the details of exactly lines and borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was in cohorts with the putschists against Yeltsin, that they maintained constant links, that they came to Belgrade, that they conferred with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I am not specifically aware of their having had contacts with Milosevic but I am aware that General Kadijevic and General Krazov, the Soviet Defence Minister, were in communication and were according, and that Kadijevic was aware of plans for a coup in the Soviet Union against Gorbachov, and also that Jovic was aware of Kadijevic's activity, but I am not certain -- I do not recall if Jovic himself had contact of that kind, but I am not aware of Milosevic having direct contact, which is not to say that he did not, just that I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that Milosevic accused even the Pope and Germany that they are, in fact, Nazis, that the world would turn against them and that it would be grateful to Serbia for its attack against the Republic of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I am aware of that kind of thing being said, but I would not... I do not have a specific recollection that it should be attributed to Milosevic which is again not to say that he did not, just that I do not have the specific recollection. (5.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Dr. Gow, in the course of the examination-in-chief, you said that you think that conflicts among the Serbs themselves would be important for these events. Do you not think that with regard to those conflicts they still agree with the basic project of a greater Serbia, so why would conflicts among the Serbs themselves be of importance? And in clarification of the events we are now referring to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that I understand what it is that you are asking of me; if you could try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. In the course of the examination-in-chief, on page 9371 and later on and a little before that, you said that for an understanding of the substance of the events and developments that occurred, it is also important to bear in mind the conflicts that existed among or between the Serbians and the Serbs. I am asking now why those possible conflicts have any importance, when in essence they agree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree that in essence there would be agreement on an overall aim. If, as I assume, I do not recall the specific reference in the testimony, but I assume with reference to differences primarily between the Pale Serbs in Bosnia and Belgrade, these were differences of tactics and style. It was a question of Belgrade's wanting what was politically advantageous at a particular moment, which meant to have apparent agreement with international concerns and proposals, so, for example, in 1994, that Belgrade appears relatively genuinely, by the assessments of all who have looked at it, to have wanted the plan on offer at that time to be accepted, and to have tried to persuade the Bosnian Serbs to accept it, without, of course, taking full measures of control, because that would have been to break down the efforts to show that they were not part of this arrangement, and that the Bosnian Serbs appear clearly to have pursued a course which Belgrade did not want, but it was not a question important enough for Belgrade at that stage to do that which it could do, to make the Bosnian Serbs fall into line. So I think the question is one of seeing that, yes, there is agreement on the overall perspective, but that at particular moments the political interests of the sides may differ slightly, of the different elements, the different Serb communities might differ slightly. I made several references to the memoirs of General Kadijevic and one of the things he points out there is that what they have achieved is that which could be achieved -- I paraphrase -- in the given international environment at that time. I would also point out, a Yugoslav, that is Belgrade, Federal Yugoslav, Serb diplomat, who, after the date and agreement put it to me that this was an agreement for now but that within five or ten years the Republika Srpska would join the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that this was all things for appearances at a certain time, but things would change at another time. So I think -- I mean, I am not sure if I have been clear and I am sorry that I have taken so long in giving the answer but I think the sense is that that is where it is important to be aware of differences, but in terms of the ideal of an overall objective, then I think broadly you would say that there would be agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Therefore it can be said that Belgrade and Pale agree in essence, and that is to create a greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Without using the term, "Great Serbia", yes. To form a set of federated territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In the course of the examination-in-chief we gathered that your position -- we will allow you to answer the question I am asking you now -- that you are not here to testify about specific events in Konjic, and Celebici, of course. Konjic, when I say Konjic, I am thinking of Celebici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is the case that I do not believe that my role is to give specific evidence either from personal experience or from investigation regarding that matter, which is not to say that, as in -- I believe, in the evidence-in-chief, as far as I recall it, I made references to certain things which I had noticed about Konjic which broadly met with the contextual evidence I was providing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we move on to another segment? You spoke at some length about history, and in the examination-in-chief in answer to questions by Mr. Niemann and also in the Tadic case you spoke about the formation of the kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenians and the idea behind it, of creating a common state. Was that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, yes I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you, Dr. Gow, do you know who chose, who elected the Yugoslav Committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will be careful and I will say, "no", but it is something that I...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Let me answer the question. No one elected it, and do you know where it was formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall it was formed in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No. In Italy. And do you know under what name it was formed, and in what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would you...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but under what name was it formed, or, to put it differently, would you agree that it was called the Croatian Committee and that it was formed in 1914?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be very careful about what I am saying, anything that I say about this. I am not sure what material relevance it will have. There was a Croatian Committee. I am not sure that I would agree that that was entirely the same thing as the Yugoslav Committee, but I really would not want to be taken... say everything with a degree of caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, Dr. Gow, that in Zagreb the Croatian, "sarbor", or Assembly, never agreed with a majority with the formation of this joint kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenians, in other words that, it never officially endorsed that state?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours... yes. I am not even sure that it is terribly interesting but it is not relevant in my submission, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this highest level tribunal in the world, certain facts are being established. My learned colleague Mr. Niemann said that he wanted to prove certain facts relevant to the history of nations. I would submit, with due respect for Dr. Gow, that in spite of the fact that he is a politicologist, that I should be allowed to draw attention to any possible errors that may have been made in the course of his testimony, not only before this Trial Chamber but also in the Tadic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, your Honours, I do not remember saying that, but if I did, I would have said it in the context of the relevance of the proceedings before you, and in any event, your Honours, this cross-examination is proceeding on the basis of a number of propositions which are being stated in the nature of giving evidence, and then seeking to ascertain whether or not Dr. Gow knows about it, but I do not think it is progressing the matter any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your permission, the Defence will also, in the course of its case, bring expert witnesses, and I see no reason why some of the theses proffered by Dr. Gow cannot be subjected to a certain degree of criticism, and for that to be done one has to investigate all the relevant circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed and let us know exactly what you are about, what actually you are driving at, I think. Let us hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. The question that I put to Dr. Gow is indeed relevant because when something is wrong at the outset, it can never become correct. In other words, if the Croatian Assembly never accepted the state of Serbs, Croats and Slovenians, then it can never, in the sense of international law, or international conventions, be treated as a lawful and legitimate state. Now, may I ask you, Dr. Gow, whether you know that the Croatian Sarbor never endorsed that state, never endorsed the decision to that effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that and I am also aware that the decision to join with the kingdom of Serbia was made, not with the reference to the Sarbor but with reference to the decision of the National Council in Zagreb which was, as I understand it, a second, in fact, National Council, and that decision was taken primarily on the basis first of all that the position of the National Council, that is to create a Slav third element within the Austro-Hungarian Empire, was not going to be achievable and that under the terms of the secret treaty in London in 1915, Italy was preparing to annex territories promised to it by the allies in Dalmatia, and therefore the decision was taken as a matter of what I would regard as expediency, to join forces with one of the other allies, being Serbia, as being the better of the likely options available. I have to say that I do not recall giving evidence about any of these matters either at Tadic or before, but simply a summary explanation of elements which fed into the formation of the -- of what was to become Yugoslavia. I am quite happy as far as I am able to deal with those things, to try and assist now, but I am not sure that what you say about things that I said in evidence before is correct. I do not recall everything that I said, of course, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Dr. Gow, please, since the formation of that Yugoslavia in 1918, do you know anything about the genocide of the Moslems, Turks, Albanians and other persecutions made in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I think it is -- it would be a matter to speak of with care. I am aware, for example, that during the course of the Second World War, that there were mass murders of Moslems in some parts, for example, of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Forcha, notably, I am aware that in the course of the Second World War and in the immediate period after the Second World War there were campaigns, I am not sure if that is the right word, against Albanians, as a result of which many went to Turkey. I am not sure what it is that you are seeking from me, but I am aware of -- if it is literally a question: am I aware of some things; then yes, I am aware of some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have spent quite a bit of time on the cessation of the existence of SFRY. I should like to ask you to help us, if you can; that the question is not when it ceased to exist, but rather when it ceased to exist in the way envisaged and required by the freely-expressed will. In other words, the Badinter Commission could only declare its death, that it no longer existed, but could we agree that it ceased to exist much before that? Long before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think one thing I do recall from testimony in the Tadic case was putting forward the view that, whilst the definitive end of the process of dissolution as per the Badinter certification of death might be 27th April 1992, that in my own view the Federation ceased to function in May 1991. If you are asking: is it possible to say that the Federation ceased to function at an earlier stage, then I would say that, again, there was a process underway from the late 1980s, elements of which contributed to that situation, and which were leading to a position in the Federation in which the Federation would cease to function, but my own view is that you can say that it ceased to function on 15th May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Therefore, until April 1992 -- we know that by then there were tens of thousands killed in Croatia, already thousands also in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and until -- it was then that the Federal authorities undertook the aggression against Croatia, Slovenia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that by then both Croatia and Slovenia had abandoned Yugoslavia, availing themselves of their constitutional right to do so. Would we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would agree that Croatia and Slovenia had taken the course of action that you suggested. Again, my own view, suspicion, would be that also the Serb leadership had done the same thing. That is the perspective of maintaining the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: That is what I wanted to ask you. Did the Serbs prevent a referendum only in their towns or in other towns as well, and places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which referendum? The referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina or...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... where it was possible to try to prevent the referendum being held, as I understand it, those efforts were made. It was primarily in Serb majority areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I have completed my cross-examination. I wish to thank you once again. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am at your pleasure. It is 5.20, I have got a few documents I want to talk about, there is nine copies of each of them. It is not that much, but do you want me to start now or do you want me to start Monday morning? In ten minutes I do not even think it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may do very little in ten minutes, and if you are continuing, well, you might as well start on Monday, except all you need to do is introduce these documents and...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, there are also some subsequent questions that are based on some of the things that he said today that I want to ask him. I know that I promised you that all I was going to do was put in documents, but some subsequent questions have come up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, before he forgets some of those questions and their answers, you might start now, in the next ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Fine your Honour, I would be happy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I have been dealing with these things on and I am just going to do without them if I can. It just seems more comfortable, without the earphones. My name is Tom Moran and I represent a man called Hazim Delic. Do you know Hazim, by the way? Have you ever seen him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that I have or I would recognise him, although I presume I might have seen him if he was in the room but I would not recognise him from anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. I am going to ask you some -- we are going to go over --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I have just identified him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. The last man over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We winked at each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. One of the things that you told Mr. Ackerman, you said that you think it is important that you understand what is asked and I think that is awfully fair, and sometimes I start talking a little faster than I think, and if sometimes my questions are not as clear as they ought to be and you have been very good about saying, "I do not understand the question", but if you do not understand the question, will you stop me and get me to rephrase it until you understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think experience would suggest that I would rather be careful and accurate than just charge in. So I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And I appreciate that, doctor. By the way, just so that I am clear in my own mind, you are here as an expert in military affairs of Yugoslavia and in political affairs of Yugoslavia as it applies to the military. Is that a fair assessment of your area of expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would regard my expertise as being in the domain of military and military/political matters and also in international matters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That is fair enough. If the usher could help me, I have a couple of documents. While these are being marked, I will just tell you where I am coming from, and what I am going to be doing with these documents so it is not going to be any surprise to anyone. There has been some dispute in this courtroom over the exact time of the demise of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and you have testified today and there is frankly -- these are documents that will probably back up your opinion. If I could have the exhibit number of the first one, the Security Council document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document number D14/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would be D40/4? Or D41/3, rather?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. If you would look at -- well, in effect, you are doing it right now. Exhibit D14/3, have you ever seen that document before? Maybe not in that particular form.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that is a copy of a letter from the charge of the SFRY to the United Nations to the present Security Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should point out, just for absolute accuracy, I have not seen the letter before but I have seen the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. You have seen the annex which is attached to this United Nations document. Would you agree with me that this is a document that is the declaration, if you would, of existence, the birth certificate of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure about the image, but yes. This is the point at which the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Serbia and Montenegro was declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And in paragraph 1 it makes a claim of being a continuation of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it makes the claim to be the legal and political successor of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The successor state.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and to be the sole successor state, but of course I am sure you are aware that that is a matter of dispute and a matter which is unlikely to be resolved for many years to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I promise you, we are headed there. Okay, document D15/3. That purports to be a copy of the constitution of the FRY, and just so you know the source of it, so that you can tell just by looking at it, it is from the Internet site that is sponsored by the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the Yugoslav government official web site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It is the official web site. That is correct. And would you agree with me that that is a copy of the constitution? There are a few typos in it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to Article 2. It is on the front page. The bottom of the front page. It defines what constitutes the FRY. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It identifies Serbia and Montenegro as being the elements which compose the FRY, and then goes on to say that other member republics may join.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Nobody has, have they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To date, not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Then let me also direct your attention to Article 17 of the constitution. That has to do with citizenship, does it not? Your Honours, it is on page 4. Basically what Article 17 says is that the FRY confers Yugoslav citizenship on its inhabitants, and that to be a Yugoslav citizen shall simultaneously be a citizen of one of the republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Then, so to be a citizen of the FRY you would have to be a citizen of either the Republic of Serbia, the Republic of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or any other eventual member... yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure, if some other member state should ever join, if...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The expression is, "may be joined...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Indicating that the Federation may allow at some future date some...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: ... sort of a joining. "May be joined".

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So one would apply for admission. Your Honours, at this point I would move admission of D14/3 and D15/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They are admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I have got a few more documents here and I think we can... I am at your pleasures, your Honour. Do you want to just run a few minutes late and get these documents in and talk about them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. With the assistance of the usher...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would I be permitted just to point something out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the context of this discussion about the inhabitants, I think I would probably also draw your attention, I was looking -- I think, I believe, as I recall, there is a similar reference in the constitution but in the declaration here in that, if you look in -- I think it is the seventh paragraph down -- in addition to the kind of provisions that you were just making, they also explicitly make a claim to continue to exercise the rights and obligations of the SFRY, vis-à-vis the territories of Krajina and other areas, so with a view to being -- that they are the responsible authorities for the inhabitants of those areas, whether or not that formally fits within the definition of the inhabitants and the composition that you have identified there. Maybe I can find it with looking, but I seem to recall that there was a similar reference in the constitution. I think it is the seventh paragraph down. It is easy. It is the second paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: "... bound by obligations"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The final sentence in the paragraph reads: "The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia shall respect and fulfil the rights and obligations of the SFR of Yugoslavia, assume vis-à-vis the territories of Krajina which have been placed within the framework of the United Nations peacekeeping operation."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, while these documents are being distributed to the court and while we are getting some numbers on them, you alluded to, a second ago, that the FRY's claim to being the sole successor state was not -- was rather controversial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a contested matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, it is contested to this great good day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suspect will be for some very long time to come. Which is a separate question, of course, from the one you raised at the beginning about an existence of a political and territorial community in the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand. Let me get some exhibit numbers when the -- in fact, you may have the originals there, in fact of you. There are four letters. The first is a note by the present Security Council. Do you have that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a note by the President of the Security Council with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: On the back there is a number. What is that number? It is D --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: D16/3. Would you care to do an exchange?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No. You have got the official one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I take on a new job as Registrar or whatever you call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And there is a letter dated 5 May 1992 from the Deputy Representative of the United States to the United Nations address to the President of the Security Council. Do you see that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a second letter. 26th May from --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It is a letter dated 5 May from the Deputy Representative of the United States.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Hold on a moment. The next one I have is Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Canada is fine. There should be two letters from Canada?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: United States. I have got United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. What is the exhibit number on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is D19/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And then you have two letters from Canada. One dated May 6th and one dated May 26th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 6th May is 18/3. And 26 is D17.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Have you ever seen these before, doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Literally, I have, yes. Because I believe you handed them to the Office of the Prosecutor, certainly the Office of the Prosecutor earlier on today, knew this had been done and just showed them to me to say that we have been given these.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, these are occasions, are they not, from various members of the Security Council at various times talking about the former SFRY, Former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I recall, looking at them and just glancing at them now, they deal with the fact of the non-recognition of the claim to be sole successor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, and well, for instance, the letter dated May 26, D/17/3 from the Canadian Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I point out that it does not have a /3 on here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It does not?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It should be /3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. It does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The Registrar will fix it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to make a note for the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That talks about the former SFRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And at the time Canada was a member of the Security Council, was it not? If you do not know, you do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall, but -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But it would surely indicate the Canadian Government at least as a member of the United Nations was contesting the right and ability of the FRY to act as the sole successor state to the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, this is the letter...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: 26th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You did it again. I am not sure that it does that. It requests that sanctions be imposed against Serbia and Montenegro because of its --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
